Straumann Holding AG · STMN-CH · Investment memo

Straumann: a top-decile franchise closing its leaks lifts EPS growth to about 10% a year, but the franc and the multiple decide the return

As at 18 November 2026. Share price CHF 107.20 (13 November 2026); market value CHF 17.1 billion. Money in Swiss francs; profit figures are on the company's core basis, which consensus uses, unless stated. Next results: 24 February 2027, the first under the new chief executive. Sources and bases are in the end notes.

Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one paragraph. Straumann, the world's largest dental implant maker, is taking share in a shrinking market, but for four years almost none of that progress reached its shareholders. Core EPS was CHF 2.72 in FY2022 and CHF 2.99 in FY2025, because the Swiss franc and a loss-making aligner business absorbed the operating gains. The case for the next 12 to 24 months is that this leakage stops. Our forecasts have core EPS of CHF 3.36, 3.68 and 4.00 for FY2026 to FY2028, growth of about 10 percent a year against about 3 percent over FY2022 to FY2025, with free cash flow more than doubling. Most of the change comes from actions already taken: aligner losses being closed down, a finished capacity programme, and tighter cost control under a new finance director. Straumann is therefore a self-help case inside a top-decile franchise, and the outside world, above all the franc, mainly decides how much of the self-help survives translation into francs.

Where the outcomes are skewed to the positive, and where they are not. The skew of outcomes is the lens that matters most for the decision, and the answer differs by layer.

Skewed positive
Guidance is skewed positive. The company guides in constant currency, which removes its largest source of variance, and it sets its guides low. FY2026 guidance will very probably be met. The first FY2027 guide is likely to repeat the inherited framework, which our forecasts meet or slightly beat, and that guide is more likely to be raised during 2027 than cut.
Skewed positive
The next two profit reports are skewed positive. The second half of 2026, reported on 24 February 2027, should show the strongest reported earnings growth since the post-Covid rebound, and the two sales updates around it lap the two weakest quarters of the cycle. By my arithmetic, currency already added to reported revenue growth in Q3 2026, after years in which it subtracted (#1).
Skewed positive
Three options that sit in no forecast are skewed positive: an exit from orthodontics, a decision to let cost savings drop through to profit, and a use for a cash balance that reaches about 8 percent of today's market value by 2030. A chief executive from outside the company, with a record of cost and cash discipline, takes charge on 1 December.
Not skewed positive
Consensus EPS in francs is not skewed positive. Our FY2027 EPS is about 6 percent below consensus and our FY2028 EPS about 10 percent below, and consensus sits at the top of our range of outcomes. One assumption, the franc, explains more than half of that gap. FY2026 free cash flow is the one near-term number likely to disappoint.
The dated test
The dated test is the second half of 2027, when a Chinese price cut, tougher comparisons, an annualising product cycle and our assumed franc drift coincide, and reported EPS growth slows to about 7 percent.

The favourable news comes first and the test comes later. That sequence is the most useful single fact for timing a position in the share.

Five judgements will move the shares most (each is worked through with arithmetic in #9): how much the franc takes; whether share gains keep organic growth near 8 percent; how much of the self-help drops through to profit under the new chief executive; how deep China's price round cuts; and whether working capital stops absorbing cash. Above all five sits the multiple, which is worth more to the return than any of them (#11, #12).

The return depends on the multiple. At Viewforth's guideline fair multiple of 35.76 times, the model gives a total return of +45.8 percent to 31 December 2027 and +62.6 percent to 30 June 2029, of which 27.5 points is re-rating. Earnings and dividends alone give about +15 percent and +28 percent, or 10 to 13 percent a year. My view is that the guideline multiple is the top of the plausible range, not its centre: our forecasts support about 29 to 32.5 times, which gives +20 to +33 percent to end-2027.

Where I differ from the market.

Lifecycle and set-up. The share is turning up with its thesis starting to broaden, one stage earlier than the dashboard's "Reinforcing". The set-up fits "a cause for concern clearing in a high-quality business on a low multiple, leading to reversion to normal", with an earnings step-up from corporate change as the mechanism underneath.

1Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

The operating environment is a mild negative for the case: the franc and consolidating buyers tax it, digital dentistry helps it, and both taxes sit near their extremes while our forecasts assume no relief.

Evidence.

  • Demand is cyclically weak. Morgan Stanley's US practitioner survey put implant demand at minus 3.6 percent in Q3 2026, with 57 percent of practices reporting fewer patient visits. Financed full-arch cases are falling hardest, and 98 percent of Straumann's sales are paid for out of pocket. China is stabilising after destocking; Europe is steady; Asia outside China is growing fast; Latin America slowed to 6.5 percent growth in Q3 as Straumann tightened credit in Brazil.
  • Competition is easing at the top and tightening below. Dentsply Sirona's implant business is shrinking at a double-digit rate. Envista's Nobel S-Series, which reached 18 percent of Nobel's premium units within six months, is the first credible premium rival product in years. Value-tier prices fall about 3 percent a year.
  • Buyers are consolidating. Dental chains place about 20 percent of implants, heading for about 30 percent by 2029, and buy at discounts of 15 to 25 percent.
  • Regulation helped 2026 and reverses in 2027. China's second round of volume-based procurement (VBP 2.0, the state's price tender for implants) slipped to early 2027, and Brazil cut its import tariff on value implants from 50 to 10 percent. The VBP 2.0 price cut is expected at 5 to 15 percent, against about 55 percent in round one.
  • The franc is the structural tax. Under 2 percent of revenue but about a fifth of costs are in francs; currency translation is unhedged; and the franc has been a headwind in eight of the last ten years.
  • Digital dentistry is the one clean tailwind, and it favours the integrated supplier.

A new data point, by inference: currency turned into a small tailwind in Q3 2026. Reported revenue growth was 4.9 percent for the first nine months against 2.3 percent at the half-year, which implies Q3 reported growth of about 10.5 percent against 9.2 percent organic. The files do not give the quarter's own reported figure, and the estimate rests on my split of last year's second half, but the result is not sensitive to that split. If the inference is right, translation has moved from a 5.5-point drag in the first half to a small tailwind, which supports our second-half revenue input and FY2026 consensus.

Inference: the two variables that hurt most are both near extremes, so external surprises from here are more balanced than their weak levels suggest. US implant demand is at its weakest survey reading in at least four years. The trade-weighted franc is not far from the all-time highs it reached early in 2026, and November bank forecasts for the franc are now roughly flat for 2027. Our forecasts assume no relief from either variable: a US market near zero growth through 2027, and a franc that drifts stronger from 2028.

So what. Straumann is not an external-forces case. External forces set the conversion rate between what the company delivers and what a Swiss-franc shareholder receives, while share gain does the work: North America grew 7.5 percent in Q3 against a market falling 3.6 percent.

Strongest counter-case. An implant procedure costs about USD 4,000 and can be deferred. In 2008 to 2009 implant demand fell 6 percent and Straumann's revenue shrank 2 percent organically. If the US consumer weakens further, share gain cannot fully offset the fall in demand, and consolidated buyers will press harder on price in a weak market.

What would change my view. Up: two consecutive improving US practitioner surveys, or the franc holding today's level through mid-2027. Down: North American growth converging on the survey's market rate, or China's tender rules favouring domestic makers.

Against the market. I agree with the market that demand is weak and not inflecting. I differ on the franc, which I see as structural rather than easing, and on emphasis: US demand, the market's largest worry, matters less to Straumann's franc earnings than the currency, the market's smallest worry.

Conclusion: The environment offers one tailwind and two persistent taxes, so this topic is a mild negative for the case, softened because the worst variables are near extremes and our forecasts assume no relief.

Score: 39, set by the Rater. The expected external forces take a clear but bounded slice: the franc subtracts about 1.5 points of revenue a year from 2028 and margin with it, US implant demand runs at -3.6%, dental chains heading to 30% of implants press price, value-tier prices fall about 3% a year and China's 2027 tender reverses this year's help, against one clean tailwind (digital) and a weakened Dentsply; the worst variables are near extremes and the forecasts assume no relief, which keeps it off the 25 level where end-market problems hit the main customer base (Straumann still grows 8-9% organically). Coherent with the External change forces group (36), a touch above it for the competitor weakness that share gain exploits; the volatility of the franc is scored in topic 9, not here.

2Internally driven corporate change

Internal change is the chief positive of the case: a broad, funded programme, mostly a matter of stopping loss-making activity, is already in the accounts and supplies about 275 basis points of margin by FY2028.

Evidence.

  • A margin programme is already in the accounts. On 17 June the company raised its FY2026 constant-currency margin guide from +30 to +60 basis points to +140 to +170. First-half operating costs fell by 130 basis points of revenue on flat headcount. The new finance director found about 16,000 vendors serving 12,000 employees.
  • The perimeter is being cut where it destroyed value. The consumer aligner brand was sold in 2024; ClearCorrect left 35 markets; the German aligner plant closed; and aligner production for Europe and Asia moved to a contract manufacturer (Smartee). Bernstein puts the orthodontics loss at CHF 60 to 70 million a year before restructuring. The company's milestones for that loss are "halved by late 2026" and "breakeven by end-2027".
  • A capex cycle has ended. More than CHF 1 billion of investment doubled implant capacity. First-half capex fell from CHF 113 million to CHF 74 million, and first-half free cash flow rose 49 percent.
  • The product cycle has a second leg. The iEXCEL implant system reached close to 40 percent of premium volumes within about 18 months, with about a fifth of its users converted from rivals. A full-arch solution that works only with iEXCEL launches in January 2027.
  • Manufacturing is moving local-for-local. The Shanghai plant is licensed and produces at about 20 percent lower cost than the Swiss sites, and the franc share of group costs is falling by about 3 points as a result.
  • The leadership is changing hands. Christopher Norbye, who doubled sales and tripled profit at Beijer Ref and released more than SEK 1 billion of working capital there in 2025, takes over as chief executive on 1 December with no dental experience. The finance director who drove the June raise stays. There have been five executive board changes in 18 months.

Inference. Three conclusions stand out.

  • The thesis needs the company to stop doing things, not to learn new ones. Straumann must stop losing money in aligners and stop building capacity, and that reliance on stopping is why the thesis is highly plausible. Even orthodontics has two routes to the same profit result: breakeven, or an exit that needs no new competence. Peers have mostly exited their loss-making adjacencies.
  • The forces are owned by people who stay. The finance director and the cost programme remain in place, so the leadership handover is a risk overlay, not the driver.
  • Four years of stagnant franc earnings produced an organisational response. The board hired an outsider with a record in costs, cash and capital deployment, into a pay scheme whose annual bonus is paid wholly on economic profit after a capital charge. That pay scheme raises the odds of more drop-through and less idle cash, whether the cash is then deployed well or badly.

So what. The internal forces supply about 275 basis points of constant-currency margin over FY2026 to FY2028, about 200 of it from orthodontics, plus the step-up in cash. The internal forces are the case.

Strongest counter-case. Much of the FY2026 margin step is timing that does not recur as a source of further gains: the Chinese tender delay and the Brazilian tariff cut account for 85 to 130 basis points on Bernstein's bottom-up split. Cost programmes at Coloplast, Dentsply Sirona and Envista were largely reinvested. The outgoing chief executive's departure is unexplained. The incoming chief executive's record includes a USD 1.3 billion acquisition funded by a rights issue, and Coloplast's two large deals cut its return on capital by two-thirds.

What would change my view. Up, on 24 February: "losses halved" confirmed with a number, wording that lets savings drop through to profit, and a working-capital target. Down: a large acquisition at a sector multiple, the finance director leaving, or the orthodontics breakeven date dropped without an exit.

Against the market. The market agrees on the self-help ("more margin upside to come"). I differ in two places. First, the first-half constant-currency margin was only 30 basis points above the prior year's, so the underlying pace of improvement is nearer 50 to 70 basis points a year than the 155 forecast for FY2026. Second, I give real weight to an orthodontics exit, which so far only former executives have voiced.

Conclusion: The internal forces are strong, broad, already delivering and mostly a matter of stopping loss-making activity, which makes this the chief positive of the case, with the new chief executive as option value that carries a cost.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. A broad, funded programme already in the accounts: the FY2026 constant-currency margin guide raised by 110bp, first-half opex down 130bp of revenue, an orthodontics loss of CHF 60-70m being halved and taken to breakeven or exit, capex down from CHF 113m to 74m, Shanghai at 20% lower cost, and a second product leg (iEXCEL at 40% of premium volume, full-arch in January), together about 275bp of margin and a doubling of free cash flow by FY2028. It is mostly repair (stopping losses and building) with some growth on top, and is held back by five executive changes in 18 months, an unexplained CEO exit, an outsider CEO with an acquisition record and a history of reinvesting savings, so it sits with the Internal change forces group (70), just above Theon and below Instalco's full reset.

3Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

The foundations are a clear positive: Straumann is a top-decile franchise by share, margin and return, with a moat widening on share and contested on price, and with cash conversion and earnings quality as its blemishes.

Evidence.

  • Position. Straumann holds about 35 percent of the world implant market, up from 29 percent in 2021, and 50 to 55 percent of the premium tier; it is about twice the size of the number two. Premium is a three-player market, while the value tier is fragmented, with more than 200 brands in Italy and Spain alone.
  • Moat. Decades of clinical evidence; a training network with more than 25,000 members and 370,000 professionals trained in 2025; about 80 percent retention of legacy surgical accounts; direct sales for about 95 percent of revenue; and 58 percent of surveyed US practitioners naming Straumann best in class.
  • Financial profile. Core gross margin of about 70 percent; core EBIT margin of about 25 percent, roughly double Envista's; return on invested capital of about 25 percent; and net cash.
  • The blemishes. Free cash flow has run at only 55 to 65 percent of core net profit after leases. Core EPS is about a third above reported EPS (CHF 2.23 in FY2025), and legal costs labelled non-recurring have recurred for three years. Receivable days have lengthened from 48 in 2021 to 76 at June 2026. Straumann's pricing power is nominal, not real (#5).
  • Management. Double-digit organic growth in 29 of the 31 quarters to 2025; share gained through a pandemic and through a 55 percent Chinese price cut; staff engagement in the top tenth of its survey universe; and an ambition of about 10 percent organic growth a year to 2030. Capital allocation has been mixed: CHF 600 to 700 million went into aligners without producing a profit, and there is no buyback.

Inference: the existence of Straumann's moat is not in question; its monetisation is. The moat is widening where it is built (clinicians, training, workflow and scale) and contested at the price frontier (chains, value brands and China). The implant industry is really two industries under one name, premium and value, and Straumann's growth mix is drifting toward the less attractive value industry. One refinement matters for monitoring: sales to chains dilute the gross margin but cost less to serve, so they are roughly neutral to EBIT. A gross margin slipping below 70 percent is therefore a warning only if the selling-cost ratio is not falling at the same time.

So what. The foundations justify a confident assumption of continued share gain and a premium multiple to the sector. They do not justify assuming real price increases, and the size of the multiple premium depends on growth (#11).

Strongest counter-case. The strongest counter-case is commoditisation. Some studies show Korean implants to be clinically equivalent; former insiders describe chains negotiating premium implants down to USD 100 to 200; and premium innovation has plateaued. The management bench that built the record is also thinner, because Straumann alumni now run Medartis.

What would change my view. Down: a core gross margin below 70 percent for two halves with selling costs flat; Nobel's conversions cutting North American growth to the market rate; or a regional head leaving. Up: receivable and inventory days falling at December 2026 against December 2025.

Against the market. I agree with the consensus on quality. Against the bearish expert narrative of "commoditising implants", the best evidence is that the core gross margin held above 70 percent through both the Chinese price cut and the 2020 collapse in volume.

Conclusion: This is a top-decile franchise by share, margin and return with a moat widening on share and contested on price, led by a strong operating team in the middle of a large handover, so the foundations are a clear positive with cash conversion and earnings quality as the blemishes.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Qualitatively strong: number one with about 35% of world implants and 50-55% of a three-player premium tier, a moat of clinical evidence, training (370,000 professionals) and 80% account retention, 95% direct sales, and a management that delivered double-digit organic growth in 29 of 31 quarters; the profile is a 70% gross margin (87th percentile) and net cash, though ROIC is 14.6% on the Universe's basis (81st percentile) rather than the memo's 25%. It is held at the 75 level by a moat that protects volume rather than price, growth drifting to chains and the value tier, 55-65% cash conversion, a third gap between core and reported EPS and poor returns on recent new capital (CHF 600-700m into aligners); I sit a little above the four groups (64-72) because a global number-one share behind clinical barriers and a stronger growth record put it level with, not below, Tenaris.

4Conservatism of guidance and the record of delivery and upgrades

Guidance is specific, conservative and reliably beaten in constant currency, but the company has not kept Swiss-franc estimates conservative, so beaten guides have coexisted with trimmed estimates.

Evidence.

  • Annual guides are set low and beaten. For FY2024 the company guided high-single-digit organic growth and delivered 13.7 percent. FY2025 came in at the upper end of the range on growth and inside the range on margin. For FY2026, a February guide that forced consensus down was raised by 110 basis points in June and confirmed in August and October. The outgoing chief executive's phrase was "planning for the worst".
  • Reported results match consensus closely. EPS has landed within about 1 percent of consensus at each of the last three year-ends, and organic growth beat consensus in each of the first three quarters of 2026.
  • Estimates a year or more out have been poor. Consensus EPS for every year from FY2025 to FY2028 has fallen by a fifth to a third from its peak (FY2026 from CHF 4.20 to 3.28), mostly because of currency. The 2021 mid-term targets were replaced, not met.
  • The mid-term ambition is mixed. The ambition of "about 10 percent" organic growth sits above the nine-month run-rate of 8.3 percent, while the margin ambition of 40 to 50 basis points a year sits below what orthodontics alone is worth.

Inference: the company is conservative where it controls the outcome (the annual guide and the margin) and not where it does not (the currency). Straumann guides the currency effect only for the current year, at spot rates, and its growth ambition keeps consensus revenue high, at about 9.4 percent organic growth for FY2027. "Operational beats, reported cuts" is therefore one mechanism, not bad luck: consensus translates a constant-currency framework at flat exchange rates, the company delivers the framework, and the franc trims the result. The proof is 2026: the margin guide rose 110 basis points, yet consensus FY2026 EPS still ended the twelve months 5.4 percent lower.

So what. Guidance events are favourable for the share. But a raised guide has not meant raised Swiss-franc estimates, and the multiple is struck on estimates in francs.

Strongest counter-case. The conservative guidance habit may have belonged to the chief executive who is leaving. New chief executives at close peers have just reset expectations: Coloplast cut its 2030 growth target on 3 November; Sonova's new chief executive stepped away from mid-term targets; and Medacta rebased its margin target. I put the chance that the "about 10 percent" growth ambition is lowered or reframed within three years at about one in three.

Why a reset is less worrying than it sounds. Coloplast's reset was received as a clearing event. The likeliest reframing for Straumann, "somewhat less growth, somewhat more margin and cash", is what our forecasts already assume. And Bernstein regards the conservative habit as the institution's rather than one person's, with the finance director who drove the June raise staying.

What would change my view. A first FY2027 guide above the framework would signal that the new chief executive is confident early. A growth guide below high single digits, or margin wording below the framework, would be a rebase, not caution.

Against the market. Deutsche Bank and Jefferies already expect a cautious first FY2027 guide, and I agree, so the guided range itself should not shock. My difference is where I expect the information to be on 24 February: in the margin wording, the orthodontics statement and what is said about cash.

Conclusion: Guidance is specific, conservative and reliably delivered in constant currency, which is a real positive, but the company has not kept Swiss-franc expectations conservative, so the record is of beaten guides alongside trimmed estimates.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. Annual guides are set low and beaten (FY2024 13.7% against high-single-digit, FY2026 margin raised 110bp and confirmed twice) and prints land within about 1% of consensus, but franc consensus for every year FY2025-28 has fallen a fifth to a third from its peak, the 2021 mid-term targets were replaced rather than met, and consensus now sits above the FY2027 framework with a new CEO setting the next guide. Conservative where the company controls the outcome but not on the line the multiple is struck on, so above the Guidance group (62) but short of Maersk's repeated low-set-and-raise record.

5Pricing power, operating and financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Profit growth comes from loss elimination and the end of the capex cycle, not from price or leverage: a real positive, but time-limited and asymmetric to the downside, and its upside depends on a management decision.

Evidence, lever by lever.

  • Price is latent, and close to zero net. Premium list prices rise 1 to 2 percent a year; value prices fall; and China takes a price cut in 2027. Group price and mix is about +0.5 to +1 percent in FY2026, slightly negative in FY2027 and about +0.3 to +0.5 percent after that. Net of wage inflation, price adds nothing to the margin.
  • Operating leverage is high in the short run, but throttled by choice. About 90 percent of costs are fixed in the short run. In growth years the realised incremental margin is only about 32 percent, because management reinvests roughly half of each incremental franc of gross profit.
  • Financial leverage is absent, and works in reverse. Net cash builds and earns about 0.3 percent, against an earnings yield near 4 percent.
  • Cost-out is real and specific. About CHF 110 to 150 million of gross savings and loss removal is identifiable by FY2028. About CHF 65 to 90 million of that should reach the constant-currency margin after the Chinese price round, mix and reinvestment, and the franc then takes about half of what remains.
  • Feedback loops reinforce the franchise. Training feeds share; the single iEXCEL surgical kit raises switching costs; and users of the cloud platform reorder more.

Inference. Four conclusions follow.

  • Straumann spends its nominal pricing power as a currency hedge. The company raises local-currency prices in markets whose inflation runs 2 to 3 points above Switzerland's, and over time the franc appreciates by about that gap. That offset is why organic growth of about 11 percent a year from FY2023 to FY2025 coexisted with flat franc EPS.
  • The outsized profit growth comes from loss elimination and lower capex, not from price or classic operating leverage. In our forecasts, revenue grows 7 percent a year to FY2028, EBIT about 9 percent, EPS about 10 percent and free cash flow about 30 percent. The gearing is modest on profit and large on cash.
  • The profit gearing is time-limited. After FY2028 the model reverts to the pace of the company's mid-term framework.
  • The feedback loops are coupled. The share-gain loop now runs through general practitioners, chains and the value tier, which is exactly where the buyer-power and receivables loops act. Extra growth therefore comes at a lower incremental margin and with longer receivable days.

So what. Upside gearing is a management decision, not a property of the business. That is why the new chief executive's stance on reinvesting savings deserves close attention.

Strongest counter-case. The gearing is asymmetric. A 3-point shortfall in organic growth costs about twice what an equal beat adds, because costs are fixed in the short run while management reinvests much of any upside (#9).

What would change my view. Evidence of real price (premium net price up 2 percent or more), or an explicit decision to let the orthodontics savings drop through to profit.

Against the market. Consensus has the FY2028 EBIT margin at 27.2 percent against our 26.5 percent. That gap is not a disagreement about levers: at the exchange rates consensus appears to assume, our own FY2028 margin would be about 27.35 percent.

Conclusion: Revenue growth converts into moderately outsized EPS growth and strongly outsized cash growth through loss elimination and the end of the capex cycle, not through price or leverage, which is a positive that is time-limited and asymmetric to the downside.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. Structurally the cost base is about 90% fixed in the short run (a 55-60% decremental margin in 2020) and CHF 110-150m of identifiable cost-out and loss removal plus training and iEXCEL switching loops are real, but price is close to zero net, financial leverage is negative (net cash earning 0.3%) and management reinvests about half of each incremental franc, so the realised incremental margin is about 32% and EPS grows only 1.4 times revenue (10% against 7%), below the Universe median of about 2. Richard's note on fixed costs lifts it above the ordinary 50, but the gearing is asymmetric to the downside and time-limited, so it sits in the low 60s, coherent with Economic strength (66) and Financial forecasts (54).

6Forecast financials

Our forecasts give EPS growth of about 10 percent a year and a doubling of free cash flow to FY2028, a clear step up on the past, in line with consensus for FY2026 and below it from FY2027, mostly because of the franc.

Our FY2026 EPS of CHF 3.36 is flattered by the lower tax rate of the reported first half; the like-for-like figure to compare with consensus is about CHF 3.31 (end note 3).

The reported margin follows a simple identity, and the identity explains four flat years. The reported margin equals last year's reported margin, plus the constant-currency gain, minus the currency drag. For four years the gain and the drag cancelled, which is why the reported margin sat between 25 and 26 percent. Our forecasts take constant-currency gains of 155, 60 and 60 basis points for FY2026 to FY2028, and currency drags of 90, 20 and 35 basis points.

Four things change against the past.

  • EPS growth triples, from 3 percent a year over FY2022 to FY2025 to about 10 percent over FY2025 to FY2028.
  • Free cash flow more than doubles, and cash conversion rises from about 55 percent of core net profit to about 89 percent. Roughly half of the improvement comes from lower capex, and most of the rest from a slower working-capital build.
  • The reported margin rises about 130 basis points by FY2028, after four flat years.
  • Organic growth is lower than in the past, at about 8 percent against 9 to 14 percent.

A smaller currency drag does most of the work in lifting EPS growth from 3 percent to 10 percent. A smaller currency drag is worth about 7 points of EPS growth a year, orthodontics about 3 and a better drop-through below EBIT about 1, while lower organic growth and slower underlying margin gains take back about 4. In francs, the CHF 1.01 of EPS added between FY2025 and FY2028 is roughly +0.80 from organic growth at a constant margin, +0.40 from margin (of which orthodontics 0.30 to 0.35), -0.34 from currency and +0.14 from the drop-through below EBIT.

The shape of EPS growth through time matters as much as its level. Reported EPS growth by half-year runs at about +26 percent in the second half of 2026, +15 percent in the first half of 2027 and +7 percent in the second half of 2027, on reported margins of about 26.0, 26.6 and 25.9 percent (chart in the summary). The second half of 2027 is the first half-year in which the margin could print flat to down year on year.

Three levers outside the base case could take EPS growth beyond double digits. The base case is just double-digit growth to FY2028, fading to 7 to 8 percent after that, and it includes none of the three levers.

  • A franc that stays where it is adds about CHF 0.25 to FY2028 EPS, which takes growth to about 12 percent a year.
  • Letting orthodontics savings drop through to profit adds about CHF 0.13 to FY2028 EPS.
  • A buyback from FY2028 adds 2 to 3 percent to EPS a year.

Together, the three levers amount in effect to the consensus path of about 14 percent a year.

Strongest counter-case. The break from history is not robust to the variable that made the history. If the franc's 2023 to 2025 rate of drag returns, EPS growth falls back to 3 to 4 percent a year.

What would change my view. The second-half 2026 margin against the guided 26 percent; the FY2027 guide; and average exchange rates at each half-year end.

Against the market. On operations we are close to consensus: at the exchange rates consensus appears to assume, our FY2027 EBIT is CHF 813 million against its CHF 814 million. Consensus is, in effect, our bull case on currency, not a different view of the business.

I have changed no forecast input. The one input I weighed is currency in the second half of 2027, where our drag of 1.8 points of revenue is harsher than the roughly 1 point that November bank forecasts imply. The difference is under 1 percent of EPS and inside the error of any currency forecast, so the input stands, but the reader should treat that leg of the forecast as leaning up against our base.

Conclusion: Our forecasts give about 10 percent EPS growth and a doubling of free cash flow to FY2028, a clear step up on the past and just double-digit, front-loaded in its optics and fading to 7 to 8 percent unless the franc holds or the cash is put to work.

Score: 69, set by the Rater. 9.6% falls in the 5-10% C band (just below the 11% Universe median), and I place it high in the band because the growth is organic with no acquisitions and the reported margin rises about 130bp after four flat years, with free cash flow more than doubling. Not at the top of the band because it is front-loaded (+12% in FY2026 fading to 7-8%), the FY2026 figure is flattered by tax (3.31 like-for-like), and more than half of the step from 3% to 10% is a smaller franc drag rather than operating gain.

7Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and narrative over 6 to 12 months

The scope for upgrades is positive for guidance and open for the narrative, but neutral-to-negative for consensus EPS in francs, which is more likely to be trimmed than raised as the second half of 2027 arrives.

The calendar puts the favourable events first. Seven dated events fall between the new chief executive's arrival on 1 December and the first-half results in August 2027; the test arrives in the second half of 2027.

Guidance has good scope to be met and raised. I put the FY2026 outcome on 24 February at about 75 percent met, 15 percent beaten and 10 percent missed. For the first FY2027 guide, there is about a 60 percent chance that the growth range sits below consensus and about a 70 percent chance that the margin wording repeats the framework; our forecasts meet or slightly beat both outcomes. During 2027, I put the chance of at least one raise at about 35 percent and of a cut at about 20 percent, and the first-half results are the most likely moment for a raise, as in 2026.

Estimates have little scope to rise on our forecasts.

  • To late April 2027, estimates should hold and perhaps drift up. Brokers are marking 2027 to current exchange rates, which help. FY2026 EPS should land within 2 percent of consensus. The currency headwind to margin is tracking at 70 to 80 basis points against the guided 80 to 100, so the second-half margin could beat.
  • On 24 February, free cash flow is the one likely miss: about CHF 369 million on our forecasts against consensus of CHF 452 million.
  • The second half of 2027 is where the trims fall. Consensus FY2027 EPS growth of 18 percent, after a first half up about 15 percent, requires the second half to grow about 21 percent, an acceleration into the hardest half of the period.
  • My odds for FY2027 consensus EPS a year from now are about three in five lower (centrally by 3 to 5 percent), one in five unchanged and one in five higher. These odds are slightly less negative than a mechanical reading of our forecasts, because bank forecasts for the franc in 2027 are now flat and the product cycle has gained a second leg.
  • The breadth of upgrades is near its peak. Six months of upgrades came from two sources that will not repeat: the June guidance raise and a franc that stopped rising. FY2027 EPS estimates are up 7 percent in six months but FY2027 sales estimates only 2 percent, so revenue expectations are untested, and revenue is where our gap to consensus sits.

The narrative has scope from three unpriced options. A statement on orthodontics options, a capital-return policy or a commitment to let savings drop through would each be new. None of the three is signalled, but all three fit the incoming chief executive's record. The narrative risks are the first prominent broker note that frames the franc as structural, a visible cash shortfall, and the optics of the second half of 2027.

Five developments would turn "held" estimates into upgrades: a franc that stands still, which shrinks our FY2027 gap to consensus to about 3 percent; a weaker franc of the kind Morgan Stanley forecasts for 2028, worth 4 to 5 percent of EPS; a US recovery as interest rates fall; a Chinese price cut near 5 percent with a volume response; and drop-through of savings to profit.

Strongest counter-case to my caution. The sell-side has been right for six months, exchange rates are currently a tailwind, and the first half of 2027 will print a margin about 90 basis points higher year on year. Upgrades could therefore run through August 2027 before anyone asks about the second half.

What would change my view. Average second-half exchange rates on 31 December, which let the currency effect be estimated before the print; the FY2027 guide; and the first sales quarter with Chinese tender prices.

Against the market. The market, with the share of buy ratings up 14 points in six months, expects upgrades to continue. I expect guidance upgrades rather than estimate upgrades, and breadth of revisions flat by spring 2027.

Conclusion: Guidance has good scope to be met and raised and the narrative has unpriced options, but consensus EPS in francs has little room to rise on our forecasts and is more likely to be trimmed in late 2027, so the upgrade skew is positive for guidance, open for narrative and neutral-to-negative for estimates.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, leans up but modestly (FY2026 met or beaten about 90%, a raise during 2027 about 35% against a cut about 20%, the first FY2027 guide likely the framework), while franc consensus EPS for FY2027 is three in five likely to be trimmed by 3-5% as the hard second half of 2027 arrives inside the window, about -0.25 of the 8% revenue growth rate (roughly the 30th-35th percentile on Richard's scale); the narrative holds unpriced options (orthodontics exit, cash use, drop-through) but none is signalled. This is the 50 level's pattern, guidance up and estimates trimmed, pulled slightly below 50 by the near-certain free cash flow miss in February and consensus sitting at the top of the memo's range, coherent with the fourth set group (40) but above it because guidance weighs most.

8Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price, and peers

Momentum in guidance, estimates and price is strong and is Straumann's own while its peers are weak: a positive for the next six months, and a source of event risk for a share priced as its sector's exception.

Evidence.

  • Guidance. Guidance was raised once and confirmed twice in five months, and organic growth accelerated in each quarter of 2026 (7.1, 8.5 and 9.2 percent).
  • Estimates. FY2027 EPS estimates are up 1, 3 and 7 percent over one, three and six months, though still 2 percent lower over twelve months. Target prices are up 8 percent in six months. The share of buy ratings is 57 percent, and the mean target is CHF 116.94. The dashboard's sell-side momentum rating is A (12 November).
  • Narrative. The sell-side's themes are "more margin upside" and "worries clearing". Investors' mood, as brokers relay it, is "good quarter, tough crowd, same debates", with defensive positioning. No director or executive has bought shares in twelve months. Investor positioning is inferred, because the files hold no direct data on it (end note 5).
  • Price. The share is up 21.5 percent in six months and 14 percent above its 200-day average, with a technical rating of A (13 November); a probable new uptrend dates only from 22 October. The 200-day average has risen in just four of the last twelve months, and the twelve-month return is 5 percent.
  • Own drivers. Over the last six months, a basket of 17 European medtech peers explains only 8 percent of the share's daily variance, the lowest share in two years. The basket's rise accounts for about two fifths of Straumann's six-month gain.
  • Peers. Peer momentum is weak: only four of the 22 stocks in the dashboard sector carry an A for earnings momentum, and four dental and medtech peers cut or reset in the last three weeks (table below).

Inference: Straumann's company-specific momentum cuts both ways. A share that moves on company news is what a delivery case wants. But the market is pricing Straumann as its sector's exception while its end-market is the same one that is hurting its dental peers, so the exception has to be re-earned at each print.

So what. Momentum supports the case through the February and April 2027 events. But the uptrend is young, at four weeks, and it has already moved the multiple from 21.6 to 24.55 times consensus earnings before the dated concerns (China's tender, US demand and the new chief executive) have cleared.

Strongest counter-case. Part of the share's rise is a rotation into healthcare that may be money leaving technology, and that rotation can reverse. Margin-led upgrades with flat revenue estimates are also the weaker kind of upgrade.

What would change my view. Down: a fall back through the 200-day average (about CHF 94), or one-month revisions turning negative. Up: new highs above CHF 109.80 after 24 February with the share of buy ratings still rising.

Against the market. I agree with the market that momentum is strong. I differ on its durability into the second half of 2027.

Conclusion: Momentum in guidance, estimates and price is currently strong and company-specific while peer momentum is weak, which is a positive for the next six months and a source of event risk for a share priced as the sector's exception.

Score: 86, set by the Rater. The sell-side measure is clearly top fifth and price momentum is strongly positive, with guidance raised once and confirmed twice and FY2027 EPS up 1/3/7% (three-month revision at the 70th percentile, about 0.4 times revenue growth); peers are weak but do not pull the letter down. I hold it at B rather than A because relative strength cannot be confirmed in the top fifth from a 5% twelve-month return, a 200-day average that rose in only four of twelve months and an uptrend only four weeks old, so it sits high in the B band.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

The case is simple to state and to track, but only moderately low-risk: its largest driver is external, its evidence arrives in one lump on 24 February, and the second half of 2027 stacks four headwinds together.

The case is simple. Four nameable items separate our forecasts from the last four years: a smaller franc drag, the end of the orthodontics loss, the end of the capex cycle and a slower working-capital build. Two of the four (orthodontics and capex) are in the company's hands and in motion. One (working capital) needs a discipline the company has not yet shown. One, the largest (the franc), is external.

The case is trackable, with gaps. Organic growth is reported by region every quarter, and the franc is visible daily. But profit is reported only twice a year, there is no separate orthodontics profit and loss, and every piece of company evidence on margin, cash, orthodontics and the new chief executive's intentions arrives on one day, 24 February. The outcomes revealed that day will therefore compound with one another.

The cone of outcomes is close to symmetric around our base but skewed down against consensus. FY2026 EPS should fall within about 2.5 percent either way of our forecast. For FY2027, roughly four outcomes in five fall between CHF 3.30 and 3.93, around our base of 3.68. Around our base the FY2027 cone is close to symmetric, because operations lean down and currency leans up. Against consensus the cone is skewed down, because consensus sits at its top. The cone narrows on known dates (24 February, the Chinese tender rules and August 2027), and by August it should be about 4 percent either way.

The five judgements, with the arithmetic

Common base for FY2027: revenue CHF 2,997 million; core EBIT CHF 787 million; tax rate 21.5 percent; 159.6 million shares. On that base, CHF 10 million of EBIT is CHF 7.9 million after tax, about CHF 0.05 a share, or 1.3 percent of EPS.

1. The franc takes little in 2027 and about 1.5 points of revenue a year from 2028.

  • One point of currency translation is 1 percent of revenue, or CHF 30 million.
  • The profit lost with that revenue at the group margin is 30 x 26.3 percent, or CHF 8 million.
  • The margin also falls by 25 to 30 basis points per point of translation, because franc costs do not shrink: a further CHF 8 million or so.
  • In total, EBIT falls about CHF 16 million (2 percent), net profit about CHF 12.5 million and EPS about CHF 0.08 (2 percent). This sensitivity reproduces FY2025, when about 4.5 percent of translation left core EBIT about 9 percent below its constant-currency level (end note 4).
  • If wrong in our favour: the franc holds today's level, a tailwind of about 1.3 points in FY2027 against our -0.25. The difference of 1.55 points gives revenue of +CHF 46 million and EPS of +CHF 0.13, to about 3.81. With no drift in FY2028 either, FY2028 EPS is about 4.25 against our 4.00.
  • If wrong against us: the 2023 to 2025 drag returns, at about 4.5 points in FY2027. That outcome is 4.25 points worse than our base: revenue -CHF 127 million, EBIT about -CHF 68 million and EPS -CHF 0.35, to about 3.33, with EBIT flat on FY2026. It is the history repeating.

2. Share gains keep organic growth at 8.25 percent in FY2027 (consensus about 9.4 percent; Morgan Stanley's bear case 6 percent).

  • One point of organic growth is 1 percent of FY2026 revenue, or CHF 28 million.
  • Upside, at the 32 percent incremental margin that management chooses: CHF 9 million of EBIT, CHF 7 million of net profit and CHF 0.04 a share (1.2 percent) per point. Growth from chains and the value tier is worth less, about CHF 0.03 a share, and absorbs CHF 5 to 8 million of working capital per point.
  • Downside, at the 55 to 60 percent decremental margin of 2020, after cost action: CHF 15 to 17 million of EBIT and CHF 0.08 a share (2.1 percent) per point. Without cost action the decremental margin is about 90 percent.
  • If growth is 6 percent: revenue -CHF 62 million; EBIT -CHF 34 to 37 million (-CHF 56 million without cost action); EPS -CHF 0.17 to 0.18 (-0.28 without cost action), to about 3.50 (3.40).
  • If growth is 9.5 percent: revenue +CHF 35 million; EBIT +CHF 11 million; EPS +CHF 0.055, to about 3.73.

3. About 60 basis points of constant-currency margin a year reaches EBIT in FY2027 and FY2028, with the orthodontics loss falling from about CHF 50 million in FY2026 to about CHF 20 million and then zero.

  • Ten basis points of margin is CHF 3 million of EBIT, CHF 2.4 million of net profit and CHF 0.015 a share.
  • If savings are reinvested (margin up 40 basis points a year, the guided pace): FY2027 EBIT -CHF 6 million and EPS -CHF 0.03. By FY2028 the gap is 40 basis points on CHF 3,192 million of revenue: EBIT -CHF 13 million and EPS -CHF 0.06, to about 3.94.
  • If orthodontics savings drop through (margin up 100 basis points a year): FY2027 EBIT +CHF 12 million and EPS +CHF 0.06. By FY2028 the gap is 80 basis points: EBIT +CHF 26 million and EPS +CHF 0.13, to about 4.13.
  • If orthodontics breakeven slips a year: FY2027 margin -30 to -50 basis points, EBIT -CHF 9 to 15 million and EPS -CHF 0.04 to 0.07.
  • If orthodontics is exited: revenue falls about 7 percent; removing a breakeven business lifts the margin by up to 2 points arithmetically (the research says 1 to 1.5 points after stranded costs); and EPS is roughly unchanged. The benefit of an exit is to the margin, the growth mix and the narrative, not to EPS.

4. China's price round costs about 60 basis points of margin in FY2027.

  • China is about 15 percent of sales, or about CHF 360 to 390 million.
  • One point of portfolio price cut is about CHF 3.8 million of revenue, which falls almost wholly to profit: CHF 3 million net, or CHF 0.02 a share, before offsets.
  • The gross cost is CHF 19 million for a 5 percent cut, CHF 38 million for 10 percent and CHF 56 million for 15 percent. Our CHF 18 million net is roughly a 10 percent cut, half offset by volume and Shanghai's lower cost.
  • If the cut is 15 percent with the same offset: EBIT -CHF 18 million against our base and EPS -CHF 0.09. With no offset: EBIT -CHF 38 million and EPS -CHF 0.19 (5 percent).
  • If the cut is near 5 percent with a volume response: EBIT +CHF 18 million and EPS +CHF 0.09.
  • If the round repeats round one's depth (about one chance in ten): a margin cost of 150 to 250 basis points, CHF 45 to 75 million of EBIT, and EPS -CHF 0.22 to 0.37 (6 to 10 percent).

5. Working capital stops absorbing cash from 2027.

  • Our forecasts put year-end working capital at 18.0 percent of revenue for December 2026, against 14.7 percent a year earlier.
  • One point of the working-capital ratio is 1 percent of revenue, or CHF 28 million of free cash flow.
  • Consensus free cash flow needs a ratio of about 15 percent, flat year on year. Three points x CHF 28 million = CHF 83 million, which is exactly the gap between consensus (CHF 452 million) and our forecast (CHF 369 million).
  • If the ratio is 19 percent, free cash flow is about CHF 341 million. If it is 16.5 percent, free cash flow is about CHF 411 million.
  • EPS does not move. The CHF 83 million gap is CHF 0.52 a share, or half a percent of the market value. The gap is small in value but large as a signal, because it tests whether buyer power is stretching receivables and whether 89 percent cash conversion from FY2027 is believable.
  • A trap in reading working capital: December is the seasonal low. The December 2026 figure must be read against December 2025, not against June 2026 (26.0 percent), or a deterioration will look like an improvement.

Below EBIT, two smaller items matter. One point of tax rate, or CHF 10 million of financial items, is each worth about 1.3 percent of EPS. Neither item is guided, and together they explain roughly 2.5 points of our FY2027 gap to consensus.

Sudden risks, cyclicality and precedents

  • Sudden and fundamental risks. A franc shock (the franc rose 17 percent in days in January 2015); a harsh Chinese tender schedule; a quality event in the premium line (low likelihood but very high cost, because the case rests on clinical trust); and a large acquisition. None of these risks is existential: Straumann has net cash, no customer above 10 percent of revenue, and China bounded at about 15 percent of sales.
  • Sudden and perceptual risks. The share trades on Morgan Stanley's quarterly survey, peer results and Chinese procurement notices, whether or not Straumann's own numbers change.
  • Cyclicality. In 2020 revenue fell 10.7 percent and the core margin fell 3.7 points, recovering within a year. The business is consumer-discretionary in its demand and defensive only in its label.
  • Sector precedents. Payer price rounds hurt most where there was no private market, as with Siemens Healthineers' Chinese diagnostics and Cochlear's Chinese revenue, which fell 27 percent after a tender. Straumann survived round one because 70 to 75 percent of China's implant market is private and has already repriced. Other precedents: a company slowing from a premium multiple is "punished twice", on earnings and on the multiple; the estimates of exporters with home-country costs follow their currency; and leadership churn has coincided with de-rating elsewhere in dental.
  • An optical trap on 24 February. A second-half 2026 margin near 26 percent will be up about 240 basis points year on year, but only because the comparison was abnormal; the increase is not a new run-rate.

Strongest counter-case to my risk reading. The drivers are few, independent of each other and mostly dated; the balance sheet is ungeared; and guidance is in constant currency. On that view Straumann is a low-risk case with one noisy external variable.

What would change my view. Lower risk: Chinese tender rules inside a 5 to 15 percent cut, a working-capital target, and a franc range that holds into mid-2027. Higher risk: a strategic pivot announced on 24 February.

Against the market. The market sees the risk in US demand, China and the chief executive. I see it in the franc, in the one-day concentration of information on 24 February, and in the stacking of four headwinds in the second half of 2027.

Conclusion: The case is simple to state and to track, with four drivers and dated tests, but only moderately low-risk, because its largest driver is external, its evidence arrives in one lump and late 2027 stacks its headwinds together.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. The memo's FY2027 EPS cone is CHF 3.30-3.93 around 3.68 (about -10% to +7%, four outcomes in five), on four nameable drivers with net cash, no customer above 10% and China bounded at 15% of sales; but the largest driver, the franc, is external and can move suddenly (17% in days in 2015), demand is consumer-discretionary (revenue -10.7% in 2020), the China tender carries a one-in-ten deep-cut tail, margin and cash are disclosed only twice a year with all evidence arriving on 24 February, and the share trades on surveys and peer news. Between the 50 and 75 levels, coherent with the Risks groups (50 and 58).

10Where the share is in its lifecycle

The share is turning up with its thesis starting to broaden, one stage earlier than the dashboard's "Reinforcing", with a dated path into a reinforcing phase through mid-2027 and a dated stalling risk after it.

The dashboard's rule says "Reinforcing"; my reading is one stage earlier: turning up, with the thesis starting to broaden.

Evidence that the share is turning up.

  • Organic growth troughed in Q4 2025 and has accelerated for three quarters.
  • A large guidance raise came five months ago and has been confirmed twice.
  • Estimates have risen for six months after years of cuts, and FY2026 will be the first year in which core EPS exceeds its FY2024 high.
  • The price uptrend is four weeks old, and the 200-day average has risen in only four of the last twelve months.

Evidence that the thesis is broadening. The drivers are multiplying: margin, cash, a second product leg, three regions growing 7.5 to 10.5 percent in Q3, and a share of buy ratings that is climbing.

Evidence that the share is not yet "Reinforcing".

  • A reinforcing phase means repeated upgrades to the numbers the multiple is struck on. Here, guidance has been raised, but consensus EPS in francs for FY2026 is lower than a year ago.
  • Investors are, on brokers' accounts, still a "tough crowd" in defensive positions, and insiders have not bought.
  • The multiple is at its two-year median, not high in its range.

The path ahead is dated at both ends. The February and August 2027 prints, with reported EPS growth of about 26 and 15 percent, could carry the share into a genuine reinforcing phase. The stalling risk also has a date: the second half of 2027.

A tension to hold. Operations are turning up while expectations are further ahead: the multiple re-rated before the dated concerns cleared, and consensus sits at our bull case. Our forecasts alone therefore leave little room for upgrades, and in this phase the upgrades have to come from the options.

Strongest counter-case. If the franc stays flat and the new chief executive lets savings drop through to profit, the dashboard's "Reinforcing" will have been right early.

What would change my view. A beat on 24 February that the market rewards, with estimates rising afterwards, would move the share on a stage. A cash miss with a growth rebase and falling estimates would mean "Stalling".

Against the market. The sell-side's rising share of buy ratings says the share is moving from broadening to reinforcing. I agree on the direction and am one stage behind on timing.

Conclusion: The share is turning up with its thesis beginning to broaden, one stage earlier than the dashboard's "Reinforcing", with a dated path into a reinforcing phase through mid-2027 and a dated stalling risk after it.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's turning up with the thesis starting to broaden rather than the computed Reinforcing: organic growth accelerated for three quarters (7.1, 8.5, 9.2%), a large guidance raise has been confirmed twice, estimates rose for six months after years of cuts and the price uptrend is four weeks old, with franc EPS still below a year ago and investors defensive. It is held below Reply's early Turning because expectations have run ahead of operations (consensus at the memo's bull case, the multiple re-rated before the concerns cleared) and the stalling risk is dated to the second half of 2027.

11The fair multiple

The guideline fair multiple of 35.76 times is, in my view, the ceiling of the plausible range rather than its centre: our forecasts support about 29 to 32.5 times.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline sets the fair two-year-forward price-to-earnings multiple at 35.76 times, the 90th percentile of the share's ten-year history, because the dashboard places the share in the Reinforcing phase. The return in #12 uses the guideline multiple.

"The multiple now" has three readings, which must not be mixed.

  • 21.5 times on the dashboard. This reading is stale: it is the September month-end figure, struck at a share price of about CHF 91.50. The dashboard's "67 percent" gap to the guideline rests on this stale reading, and so does its valuation rating of A.
  • 24.55 times on FactSet consensus earnings today, between the 10th and 20th percentile of ten years.
  • 28.0 times on our own earnings, the model's basis, at about the 37th percentile. The guideline is 27.5 percent above this reading, and that 27.5 percent is the re-rating that enters the return.

The ten-year record sets a high bar for 35.76 times (monthly data, consensus basis).

  • The multiple was at or above 35.76 times in 23 of 120 months. Twenty-one of those months fell between July 2020 and March 2022, the zero-interest-rate rebound. The other two were single months: June 2023 and March 2024.
  • In the 41 months before Covid, when the research has EPS growth at 15 to 20 percent, the multiple never exceeded 32.9 times, and its median was 29.3 times.
  • Since April 2022 the median has been 27.7 times, and since March 2024 the highs have fallen in steps: 36.6, 32.7, 30.3 and 26.4 times.
  • On our earnings, therefore, the share already trades at about its post-2022 median.

My view: the guideline is the top of the plausible range, not its centre.

  • Our forecasts support about 29 to 32.5 times, the range from the ten-year median to the 75th percentile, which is also the range from the pre-Covid median to the pre-Covid high. That range suits a business growing organically at 8 percent with EPS growth of about 10 percent, turning up but not yet in peak delivery.
  • 35.76 times needs the bull case: organic growth back at 10 percent or more, rising franc estimates, and a use for the cash or an orthodontics exit. Both post-2022 touches of that level came in years of about 10 and 14 percent organic growth.
  • What ends the falling highs is franc EPS making new highs, which starts with FY2026. New EPS highs argue for some re-rating; they do not argue for a top-decile multiple.
  • A cross-check. The guideline applied to our earnings today gives about CHF 137 to 142 a share, roughly the highest broker target (CHF 136). The mean broker target implies about 27 times consensus earnings.
  • A point about the earnings basis. The guideline's history is on consensus earnings, while the model applies it to our earnings, which are lower. If consensus converges on our numbers the two bases meet; until then, the same multiple is a more demanding claim when applied to our earnings.

Strongest counter-case. The share did reach about 36 times twice in the last three and a half years, in a worse interest-rate environment than 2020 to 2021, on growth not far above today's. If the worries clear and franc EPS compounds at 10 percent, with FY2026 marking a new high, a return to that multiple is not fanciful.

The downside multiple. The research puts a fair trough at 18 to 20 times consensus earnings that are 5 to 10 percent lower than today's, which gives a share price of CHF 70 to 85.

What would change my view. Toward the guideline: a guide and prints that lift franc estimates, plus a capital-return or portfolio decision. Away from the guideline: estimate cuts in late 2027 with organic growth below 8 percent.

Against the market. Broker target multiples (mostly 23 to 28 times FY2027 earnings, in the cases I can see) sit far below the guideline, and on consensus earnings the market calls the share cheap. On our earnings the multiple is about average, so I am less convinced than the market that the starting multiple is low.

Conclusion: The guideline fair multiple of 35.76 times is in my view the ceiling of the plausible range, since our forecasts support about 29 to 32.5 times and the guideline level needs double-digit organic growth, rising franc estimates and a use for the cash.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Cheap on measure 1 with measure 2 unreadable gives B, judged on measure 1 alone. I place it at the floor of the band because much of the cheapness is deserved or stale: the 2nd-percentile reading rests on the September price (21.5x); today's 24.55x consensus is the 10th-20th percentile and 28x on the memo's earnings is about the 37th, and the ten-year history includes the zero-rate years and a 15-20% growth regime against today's 8% organic.

12Total shareholder return

The multiple decides the return: the business earns 10 to 13 percent a year for a shareholder at an unchanged multiple, my weighted expectation is about +20 percent to end-2027, and the guideline's +45.8 percent is the bull case.

The model's return at the guideline multiple, from today's share price of CHF 107.20 (the horizons are the model's fixed columns; end note 6).

Three things drive the return.

  • Earnings. Our two-year-forward EPS rises from about CHF 3.83 today to about 4.31 at end-2027 and about 4.78 by mid-2029, which is the 10 percent compounding of #6.
  • The multiple. The multiple rises from 28.0 to 35.76 times by end-2027 and is then held. The re-rating supplies three fifths of the first-horizon return and a little under half of the second.
  • Dividends. Dividends of CHF 1.10 and 1.22, then 1.32, add about 1 percent a year.
  • Without re-rating, the return is about +15 percent to end-2027 and +28 percent to mid-2029, or 10 to 13 percent a year. That is what the business itself earns for a shareholder: EPS growth plus a 1 percent yield.

The return at other multiples, to end-2027 on our earnings.

  • Each turn of the multiple is worth about CHF 4.30 a share, or 4 percent of today's price. One turn is worth roughly as much as moving FY2027 organic growth by 2 points.
  • The spread of returns across the table, about 47 points, is nearly three times the width of the EPS cone. The forecasts are more predictable than the share price.
  • The downside is real: with EPS 5 percent lower and the multiple at 24 times, the return is about -6 percent, and the research's fair trough of CHF 70 to 85 is a loss of 20 to 35 percent.

My weighting gives an expected return of about +20 percent to end-2027, as a judgement and not a forecast. I weight a bear case (24 times on lower earnings) at one in five, a base case (28 to 30 times) at one in two and a bull case (32.5 to 35.76 times) at three in ten. Together these give about +20 percent to end-2027, roughly 17 percent annualised. The guideline return is the bull case.

Three years out, the unused cash matters. By mid-2029 net cash is about CHF 0.9 billion, and nothing in the return uses it. A CHF 1 billion buyback at today's price would retire about 5.8 percent of the shares and lift EPS by 5.5 to 6 percent. That buyback is upside to the three-year earnings leg that the model does not count.

Strongest counter-case. At the last memo's price of CHF 92.16, the same business offered about 17 percent a year without heroic assumptions. The share has since risen 16 percent with no new clearing of the concerns, so part of the return has already been collected.

What would change my view. The multiple is the judgement to revisit after 24 February. If franc estimates rise after that print, the upper rows of the return table become the centre of the range.

Against the market. Broker targets (mean CHF 116.94, median CHF 120) imply a return of about 10 to 13 percent over twelve months including the dividend. The model at the guideline multiple implies three to four times that return. The whole difference is the multiple; the earnings views are close.

Conclusion: At the guideline multiple the model gives +45.8 percent to end-2027 and +62.6 percent to mid-2029, but 27.5 points of each is re-rating, so the return is solid at 10 to 13 percent a year if the multiple merely holds and exceptional only if the bull case arrives.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. About +20-23% sits at the floor of the B band, mapping to about 75-78 on the scale, and the three-year check is supportive at 10-13% a year from earnings and dividends alone. I keep it low in the band because the central case still needs a modest re-rating from 28x, the 13-month figure overstates the 18-month weighting only slightly, and the lower tail is fat (bear case at one in five near -1% to -6%, the research's fair trough at -20% to -35%).

13Summary conclusion

What this is. Straumann is a top-decile franchise that has compounded for four years without paying its Swiss-franc shareholders, and it is now closing the leaks that caused the shortfall. The change is mostly internal, mostly done, and mostly a matter of stopping things: aligner losses, capacity building and loose procurement. That is why the operating case is well founded.

What it is not. Straumann is not a demand case, a pricing case or a case that consensus is too low. On operations we agree with consensus. In francs we are 6 and 10 percent below consensus for FY2027 and FY2028, the two years that set the multiple, and one variable, the franc, explains most of that gap.

Where the skew is. The skew is positive for guidance, for the next two profit reports and for the options under a new chief executive that no forecast holds. It is neutral-to-negative for consensus EPS in francs. The favourable events come first (24 February, late April and August 2027); the test comes in the second half of 2027.

What decides the return. The multiple decides the return, more than any forecast. The business earns about 10 to 13 percent a year for a shareholder at an unchanged multiple. The guideline multiple turns that into 40 percent annualised to end-2027, but it needs the bull case to do so.

What to watch, in order.

  1. Average second-half exchange rates on 31 December, which give the first estimate of the currency effect.
  2. China's tender rules in Q1 2027.
  3. On 24 February: the second-half margin against 26 percent; December working capital against last December; the orthodontics statement; the margin wording in the FY2027 guide; and any word on cash.
  4. North American growth against the Morgan Stanley survey each quarter.
  5. The second half of 2027, when four headwinds coincide.

The four memo ratings.

60

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 60, set by the Rater. Strong, evidenced internal forces (72) are already in the accounts and triple EPS growth from about 3% to about 10% with free cash flow doubling, but the external forces are a net tax (39) and the resulting profit growth (C, about 9.6% a year) only reaches about the Universe median and rests more than half on a smaller franc drag, so this is a clear positive input that lifts profits to median growth, in the low 60s, below the memo's B.

76

Foundations' Robustness: 76, set by the Rater. A top-decile franchise on share, gross margin and balance sheet with a moat widening where it is built (Quality 76), with a reliable record of beating constant-currency guides but not of keeping franc estimates conservative (Guidance 68); held at the 75 level by a moat that protects volume rather than price, weak cash conversion, the core-reported gap and a consumer-discretionary demand base, which is the memo's B.

70

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 70, set by the Rater. The case fits 'cause for concern clearing in a high-quality business on a low multiple, reverting to normal' with a corporate-change earnings step-up underneath, and the quality and dated concerns (China tender, US demand, new CEO) are present; but the largest concern, the franc, is structural rather than clearing, demand is more cyclical than the setup's low-cyclicality label, and today's cash-conversion and receivables problems blur the mechanism, so it sits just below the 75 level for a quality business with its concern clearing (the partial re-rating is timing and is not counted here).

58

Case Riskiness: 58, set by the Rater. Simple and trackable on four drivers with net cash and constant-currency guidance (Riskiness 57), and the multiple is low in its range on consensus; but the largest driver is an unguided, sudden external variable, end-market weakness coincides with an outsider CEO following a long-tenured one, the evidence arrives in one lump on 24 February and the share trades on sentiment with a 20-35% fair trough, so the risks are more than paper cuts and it sits just above the 50 level, near the memo's C.

End notes

  1. Source check. As the file caution asked, the sources were checked: the file labelled "latest Earnings Review" covers the Q1 2026 sales update, not the half-year. The latest full results are for the first half of 2026 (19 August 2026), and the latest data point is Q3 2026 sales (28 October 2026).
  2. "Our forecasts" are the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). Money is in Swiss francs, and profit figures are on the company's core basis, which consensus uses, unless stated.
  3. FY2026 EPS basis. The model's FY2026 EPS of CHF 3.36 holds the reported first half at its lower tax rate; the like-for-like figure against consensus is about CHF 3.31. The model's history columns are on a different basis, so its "+37 percent" EPS growth for FY2026 is a change of basis, not growth.
  4. Currency rule. The files also carry a cruder rule of thumb, that a 5 percent move in the franc changes EPS by 3.5 percent. The memo uses the model's structure instead.
  5. Investor positioning. The files hold no direct data on the share register, short interest or fund flows, so investor positioning in #8 and #10 is inferred from brokers' accounts.
  6. Return horizons. The return horizons are the model's fixed columns, so the first horizon ends about 13 months from today, not 18.
  7. Return split. Earnings and the multiple compound with each other; dividends add. Use this forward-basis split, not the template's trailing one, which is distorted by the change of earnings basis.
  8. Default visuals and tables were drawn from model update 2 (FactSet data; the Master Dashboard's price and valuation charts). Each figure's own note gives its basis.
  9. Charts drawn for this page (the half-year path, the margin identity, the EPS bridge, the FY2027 EPS cone, working capital, the multiple scale) take their figures from the memo; working capital history is from the recent-periods table; brokers' FY2027 EPS from FactSet's broker sheets. The free cash flow and net cash chart in #6 takes its figures from the forecast table in #6 and FY2026 consensus free cash flow from FactSet.
  10. Text visuals (scorecards, comparison tables, timelines, probability bars) restate figures and judgements in the memo; where a figure is derived (the remainder of stated odds, the "other" margin sources, the return grid's EPS-sensitivity columns) the visual says so.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
